name: Manikandeswarar Temple, Thirumalpur
deity: Shiva as Manikandeswarar, the jewel-throated lord, with the Goddess Anjanakshi (Karunai Nayagi)
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu, the Thirumarperu of the Tevaram, sung by Appar and Sambandar (7th century); Pallava and Chola inscriptions
summary: At Thirumalpur, the town named for Vishnu's worship, Shiva as Manikandeswarar is remembered as the Lord who accepted Vishnu's own eye in place of a missing flower and gave him the Sudarshana discus.

sections.history: Thirumalpur is a small town of Ranipet district, between Kanchipuram and Arakkonam, known in the Tevaram as Thirumarperu. Its temple to Shiva as Manikandeswarar is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and a Paadal Petra Sthalam of Thondai Nadu, honoured with six pathigams — four by Appar and two by Sambandar — and the Periya Puranam tells that Sundarar too came here to worship. The stone temple is believed to have been raised under the Cholas in the ninth century. A record of the Pallava-period king Parthivendravarman speaks of the building of the temple and its enclosing verandah, and on the north wall of the central shrine is an inscription of Uttama Chola, one of a line of Chola records that follow.
sections.architecture: The temple is entered through a tiered rajagopuram and laid out in the Dravidian manner, the sanctum of Manikandeswarar at its heart and the Goddess Anjanakshi, also called Karunai Nayagi, the lady of compassion, in her own shrine. Because the shrine's story is the story of Vishnu's devotion, Vishnu's worship of Shiva is remembered in the life of the temple, shaping its festival calendar as well as the name of the town.
sections.legends: The town's name means the place of Thirumal — Vishnu. The sthala purana tells that Vishnu's discus was blunted against the adamantine body of the sage Dadhichi, and to win a new weapon he came here to worship Shiva, offering a thousand flowers each day. One day Shiva hid a single bloom; finding the count short, Vishnu plucked out one of his own lotus eyes and offered it to complete the worship. Moved by such devotion, Shiva restored him and bestowed the Sudarshana chakra, the discus Vishnu carries still.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps six daily rituals and three annual festivals. Maasi Magam, Aadi Pooram, Aani Thirumanjanam and Navarathri for the Goddess are among the notable occasions, and during the Brahmotsavam a Garuda Seva is held for Vishnu — rare in a Shiva temple — recalling his worship here. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Thirumalpur is a place where the two great traditions meet: devotees of Shiva come to the Lord who gave the discus, and devotees of Vishnu come to honour the god who gave his eye in worship. Many recite Appar's and Sambandar's hymns before the sanctum, and the temple is easily joined to a visit to Kanchipuram to the south.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals and the festival bronzes.
visit.gettingThere: Thirumalpur lies about 15 km north of Kanchipuram and a similar distance south of Arakkonam, and has its own railway station on the Kanchipuram–Arakkonam line. Buses run from Kanchipuram and Arakkonam; Chennai International Airport is the nearest airport.
